title: Dividing fractions: how many groups, how much in one group
summary: Small groups decide whether each kitchen story asks how many groups or how much in one group, model it with a tape diagram, and explain the quotient before using any rule.

standard.text: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions.

discourse: Interpret a division story as a how-many-groups question or a how-much-in-one-group question, and say which words in the story decided it.
Explain a model (tape diagram or number line) that shows why the quotient makes sense before naming a procedure such as multiplying by the reciprocal.
Check the size of a quotient against the story: dividing by a fraction less than 1 gives a quotient greater than the starting amount (3 ÷ 3/4 = 4).
sentence: Division read as a question: 3 ÷ 3/4 means How many three-fourths are in 3?
Reasoning with since and so: Since each smoothie uses 3/4 cup, 3 cups make 4 smoothies.
Conditional statements that link fit and divide: If 1/8 fits into 3/4 six times, then 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6.
word: Fraction names spoken aloud: three-fourths, one-eighth, four-fifths (ordinal words used as fraction denominators, plural with s when the numerator is more than 1).
Divided by versus into: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 can be said 3/4 divided by 1/8 or how many 1/8 fit into 3/4; the order of the numbers flips in the second phrase.
Quotient, dividend, divisor and reciprocal, with flip avoided as the only explanation.

contentObjective: Students will interpret and compute quotients of fractions and solve word problems by modeling division of fractions with tape diagrams.
languageObjective: Students will explain whether a division story asks how many groups or how much in one group, using How many ___ are in ___? and since/so statements tied to a model.

L1-2: It is ___ groups. (Word bank: groups, fit, cup, three-fourths, one-eighth)
L3-4: This story asks how many ___ are in ___, so I divide ___ by ___.
My tape diagram shows that ___ fits into ___ ___ times.
L5-6: The quotient is greater than the dividend because the divisor is less than 1, which means ___.
This story asks how much is in one whole group, so ___ ÷ ___ tells ___.
Multiplying by the reciprocal works here because ___, and my model confirms it by ___.

vocabulary.definition: the answer to a division problem
the amount being divided; the first number in a ÷ b
vocabulary.morphology: from Latin dividendum, 'the thing to be divided'

vocabulary.definition: the number you divide by; the size of one group or the number of groups
the number that multiplies with a given number to make 1; the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3
a set of things counted together as one
the amount for one person or one use, such as one serving
to go into a space exactly; how many times one amount goes into another
vocabulary.morphology: also means healthy or the right size for clothing; ask which meaning fits

activity.title: Kitchen Division Stories
steps: Write the three story problems below on the board. Each group of three tears a long strip of paper for tape diagrams. Roles: Reader, Modeler, Explainer; rotate for each story.
The Reader reads one story aloud. The group writes it under one of two headings on their paper: How many groups? or How much in one group? The Explainer names the words in the story that decided it.
The Modeler folds or marks the paper strip to show the story, saying the division as a question (How many one-eighths are in three-fourths?).
The Explainer states the answer with a since/so sentence. Only then does the group check with the reciprocal and compare the two methods.
Exit talk: each group answers why 3 ÷ 3/4 is bigger than 3, using one frame from the L5-6 band if possible.

problems.prompt: You have 3 cups of yogurt. Each smoothie uses 3/4 cup. How many smoothies can you make?
How many 1/8-cup scoops of cocoa are in 3/4 cup?
Four-fifths of a bag of flour weighs 2 pounds. How much does a full bag weigh?
problems.answer: 2.5 pounds, or two and a half pounds

warmup: Write 1/2, 3/4, 1/8, 2/3 and 4/5 on the board. Partners take turns reading each fraction aloud in full (one-half, three-fourths, one-eighth, two-thirds, four-fifths), then ask each other How many ___ are in 1 whole? for three of them. Listen for the s on fourths and fifths when the top number is more than 1.
